explanations.answer: Carry out His anger and rebuke
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The verse says the LORD will come with fire, and His chariots are like a whirlwind. He comes "…to execute His anger with fury and His rebuke with flames of fire." (Isaiah 66:15) This is a heavy picture, and the text doesn't soften it.

explanations.answer: Rest in a house built for Him
explanations.explanation: A house for resting is a nice thought, but that's not what this verse says. The LORD comes with fire, and His chariots are like a whirlwind. He comes "…to execute His anger with fury and His rebuke with flames of fire." (Isaiah 66:15) This is a heavy verse, and it says nothing about a house.

No headcount in this verse, friend. The LORD comes with fire, and His chariots are like a whirlwind. He comes "…to execute His anger with fury and His rebuke with flames of fire." (Isaiah 66:15) Counting people isn't what the text describes.

Right on the money, baker. The verse says, "For by fire and by His sword, the LORD will execute judgment on all flesh, and many will be slain by the LORD." (Isaiah 66:16) Fire and sword, and it reaches all flesh. It's a serious line, so I'll let it be serious.

This one is true, friend. Isaiah 66:16 says, "For by fire and by His sword, the LORD will execute judgment on all flesh…" Fire and sword are both right there in the verse. I think it's a hard one to read, and it's meant to be taken seriously.

Yes, baker. The LORD declares that those who consecrate and purify themselves to enter the groves, following one in the center of those who eat the flesh of swine and vermin and rats, "…will perish together…" (Isaiah 66:17) All that preparing, and it's aimed at the wrong place. The text says they perish together.

This one is true, friend. The LORD says, "Those who consecrate and purify themselves to enter the groves… will perish together," declares the LORD. (Isaiah 66:17) The text says they perish together. It's a heavy verse, and it doesn't soften it.
That's it, baker. The LORD says He is "…coming to gather all nations and tongues…" (Isaiah 66:18) Tongues just means languages. So the guest list is wide open, and no language is left off it.

Moab is a good guess, friend, but the LORD's list is much bigger than one place. He says, "I… am coming to gather all nations and tongues…" (Isaiah 66:18) That's all nations and all tongues, not one country's cities.
Judah is a fair guess, friend, but the verse reaches wider. The LORD says He is "…coming to gather all nations and tongues…" (Isaiah 66:18) That's way more than one kingdom's towns.
Yes, baker. The LORD says all nations and tongues "…will come and see My glory." (Isaiah 66:18) His glory is the thing the verse says they will see. That's your answer.
Babylon is a fair guess, friend, but it's not what this verse says. After the LORD gathers all nations and tongues, they "…will come and see My glory." (Isaiah 66:18) The verse names His glory.
The ark is a fair guess, but it's not in this verse. The LORD says the gathered nations and tongues "…will come and see My glory." (Isaiah 66:18) His glory is what the verse names.
Not quite, friend. The LORD says the islands far away "…have not heard of My fame or seen My glory." (Isaiah 66:19) So the verse says they haven't heard or seen it yet. That makes this one False.

Right, baker. The verse describes "…the islands far away who have not heard of My fame or seen My glory." (Isaiah 66:19) They haven't heard it yet. The same verse says the LORD will send survivors to the nations.
That's the word, baker. The LORD says, "So they will proclaim My glory among the nations." (Isaiah 66:19) To proclaim is to announce it out loud. These survivors go out and speak it.
Seeking is a fine thing to do, friend, but it's not the word here. The verse says, "So they will proclaim My glory among the nations." (Isaiah 66:19) Proclaiming is speaking it out loud.

Guarding sounds like a job for someone standing at a door, friend. The text sends these survivors out, not posting them anywhere. "So they will proclaim My glory among the nations." (Isaiah 66:19) They carry the news to people who haven't heard it.

Yes, baker. The LORD says they'll be brought "…to My holy mountain Jerusalem…" (Isaiah 66:20) The verse lists horses, chariots, wagons, mules and camels. That's a whole parade, all headed to one place.
Samaria is a good guess, friend, but the LORD names another place. He says the brothers will be brought "…to My holy mountain Jerusalem…" (Isaiah 66:20) That's the destination in this verse.

Bethel is a fair guess, baker, but the LORD gives a different address. He says they'll come "…to My holy mountain Jerusalem…" (Isaiah 66:20) I once spent years in a junk drawer, so I know what it's like to be sure you're in the right place and be totally off. Bethel's not it this time, friend.

explanations.answer: Bring an offering in a clean vessel
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The LORD says it's "just as the Israelites bring an offering in a clean vessel to the house of the LORD." (Isaiah 66:20) So the brothers are the gift, and the LORD compares it to an offering brought in a clean vessel.

explanations.answer: Carry the ark on long poles
explanations.explanation: Carrying the ark is a fair guess, baker, but that's not the comparison the LORD makes here. He says it's "just as the Israelites bring an offering in a clean vessel to the house of the LORD." (Isaiah 66:20) The comparison is about bringing an offering.

explanations.answer: Wave palm branches at a feast
explanations.explanation: Palm branches make a nice festival picture, friend, but they're not in this verse. The LORD says the gift comes "just as the Israelites bring an offering in a clean vessel to the house of the LORD." (Isaiah 66:20) So the picture here is an offering carried in a clean vessel. Save the palm branches for another day.

Yes, baker. The LORD says, "And I will select some of them as priests and Levites…" (Isaiah 66:21) Priests and Levites are the two roles named. And notice who does the selecting: the LORD says He will.

Kings and judges both lead, friend, but those aren't the jobs named. The LORD says, "And I will select some of them as priests and Levites…" (Isaiah 66:21) Priests and Levites are the two roles in the verse.

Scribes and elders sound official, baker, but neither title is in this verse. The LORD says, "And I will select some of them as priests and Levites…" (Isaiah 66:21) Priests and Levites, that's the list. I'd love a title like that on my apron, but the verse only gives these two.

That's right, friend. The LORD says, "For just as the new heavens and the new earth, which I will make, will endure before Me… so your descendants and your name will endure." (Isaiah 66:22) The promise is tied to something He makes. So the name endures as long as the new heavens and new earth do.

This one is true, baker. The LORD declares that just as the new heavens and the new earth will endure before Him, "so your descendants and your name will endure." (Isaiah 66:22) It's a promise, and He is the One making it.

Not quite, friend. The LORD says, "From one New Moon to another and from one Sabbath to another, all mankind will come to worship before Me…" (Isaiah 66:23) The word is all mankind, not only Israel. The circle is bigger than it looks.
Right, baker. The LORD says, "…all mankind will come to worship before Me…" (Isaiah 66:23) It happens from one New Moon to another and one Sabbath to another. It's not only Israel.

explanations.answer: The corpses of those who rebelled
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker, and it's a heavy one. The LORD says, "As they go forth, they will see the corpses of the men who have rebelled against Me…" (Isaiah 66:24) I think this verse is meant to be taken seriously. The text doesn't make it light, so I won't either.

A shining temple would be a lovely sight, friend, but it's not in this verse. The LORD says the worshipers "…will see the corpses of the men who have rebelled against Me…" (Isaiah 66:24) It's a hard ending, and the text says it plainly.

explanations.answer: A river flowing from the mountain
explanations.explanation: A river is a peaceful picture, baker, but it doesn't appear here. The LORD says, "As they go forth, they will see the corpses of the men who have rebelled against Me…" (Isaiah 66:24) It's a heavy verse, and the text states it plainly.

The verse says the opposite, friend. The LORD says of the rebels, "for their worm will never die, their fire will never be quenched…" (Isaiah 66:24) Never quenched means it doesn't go out. This is a heavy line, and the text means it.

Right, baker. The LORD says, "…their worm will never die, their fire will never be quenched, and they will be a horror to all mankind." (Isaiah 66:24) Never quenched means it isn't put out. It's a heavy way to end the book, and I won't dress it up.
